title: Purim: two gifts to the poor
hook: give to at least two poor people; Maimonides says this outranks the feast

segments.voice: Yesterday, v'nahafoch hu, the day of destruction turned over. Your line was turned upside down. Today, what Purim asks you to do with your hands.

If you've been near a Jewish community on Purim, you've probably seen the baskets. Neighbors trading plates of triangle cookies, wine, fruit and candy, sometimes with themes and matching costumes. Kids running them door to door. It's the most visible thing people do on Purim. But the book of Esther lists four things for the day, and the baskets are only one of them. Another is easy to miss, because it's done quietly and nobody puts it on a doorstep. And one of the greatest Jewish legal minds said it's the one that matters most.
screen: `BASKETS ON EVERY DOORSTEP.` → `FOUR THINGS FOR THE DAY.` → `ONE THAT'S EASY TO MISS.`

segments.voice: In chapter nine, Mordecai writes to the Jews of every province. They're to keep these days with feasting and gladness, sending portions to one another, and, in the old Jewish translation, "gifts to the poor." In Hebrew, matanot la'evyonim. Evyon is a word for someone in real need, someone who has to ask. The Talmud reads the plurals closely. Gifts, at least two. To the poor, at least two people. So the minimum is one gift each to two people in need, enough to help them have a Purim meal. Then comes a rule almost opposite to how giving usually works. On Purim, the codes say, you don't investigate. Whoever stretches out a hand, you give to. Then Maimonides. In his law code, after listing the Purim obligations, he says it's better to spend more on gifts to the poor than on your own feast, or on the baskets for your friends. There is no greater and more splendid joy, he writes, than gladdening the hearts of the poor, the orphans, the widows and the strangers. Someone who does, he says, is like the divine presence, which the prophet Isaiah describes as reviving the spirit of the lowly. So the feast is real, and the baskets are real. But the gift that outranks them goes to someone who won't send anything back. Many people give on the morning of Purim itself, often through their synagogue or a local fund, so the money arrives in time for the meal.
screen: `GIFTS TO THE POOR.` · `TWO GIFTS, TWO PEOPLE.` · `WHOEVER STRETCHES OUT A HAND.` · `MAIMONIDES: THE GREATEST JOY.` · then, large: `TWO GIFTS TO THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people, or two causes, who could use something: a neighbor who's struggling, a food bank, a colleague who's quietly overwhelmed. It doesn't have to be money; it can be a meal, an hour, a ride. Picture each gift reaching them.
Matanot la'evyonim. Gifts to the poor: at least two, to at least two people, on Purim day. Today's word.
Your line: two gifts to the poor. On Purim, whoever stretches out a hand is given to. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Purim day, Jews give at least one gift of money or food to each of at least two poor people, often through a synagogue or charity fund so it arrives in time for the Purim meal, alongside sending food portions (mishloach manot) to friends.
